claim: Collective cell migration is fundamental for the development of organisms and in the adult for tissue regeneration and in pathological conditions such as cancer.
source: Collective cell migration is fundamental for the development of organisms and in the adult for tissue regeneration and in pathological conditions such as cancer.
evidence: This is a general statement about collective cell migration supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: N-cadherin regulates both adhesion and repulsion processes during Schwann cell collective migration.
source: Here we show that the cell–cell interaction molecule, N-cadherin, regulates both adhesion and repulsion processes during Schwann cell (SC) collective migration, which is required for peripheral nerve regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including knockdown experiments and functional assays.

claim: The repulsion process mediated by N-cadherin is independent of N-cadherin trans-homodimerisation and the associated adherens junction complex.
source: However, distinct from its role in cell–cell adhesion, the repulsion process is independent of N-cadherin trans-homodimerisation and the associated adherens junction complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mixing experiments and rescue experiments with N-cadherin domain constructs shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The extracellular domain of N-cadherin is required to present the repulsive Slit2/Slit3 signal at the cell surface.
source: Rather, the extracellular domain of N-cadherin is required to present the repulsive Slit2/Slit3 signal at the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments showing the extracellular domain is sufficient for CIL (Figure 3) and immunofluorescence showing Slit2/3 localization depends on N-cadherin (Figure 5).

claim: Inhibiting Slit2/Slit3 signalling inhibits CIL and subsequently collective SC migration, resulting in adherent, nonmigratory cell clusters.
source: Inhibiting Slit2/Slit3 signalling inhibits CIL and subsequently collective SC migration, resulting in adherent, nonmigratory cell clusters.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Slit2/3 knockdown experiments and recombinant Slit2 treatment shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Inhibition of Slit2 decreased SC collective migration and increased clustering of SCs within the nerve bridge in ex vivo explants from mice following sciatic nerve injury.
source: Moreover, analysis of ex vivo explants from mice following sciatic nerve injury showed that inhibition of Slit2 decreased SC collective migration and increased clustering of SCs within the nerve bridge.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo imaging experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Peripheral nerve is one of the few tissues in the mammalian adult that retains the ability to regenerate following an injury.
source: Peripheral nerve is one of the few tissues in the mammalian adult that retains the ability to regenerate following an injury (Jessen et al., 2015; Poss, 2010; Zochodne, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Successful regeneration of a transected nerve requires the collective migration of cords of Schwann cells that transport re-growing axons across the injury site.
source: We have previously shown that the successful regeneration of a transected nerve requires the collective migration of cords of Schwann cells (SCs) that transport re-growing axons across the injury site (Parrinello et al., 2010; Stierli et al., 2019; Stierli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: SC cords gain directionality across the wound by migrating along a newly formed polarised vasculature, which develops prior to SC migration.
source: Moreover, SC cords gain directionality across the wound by migrating along a newly formed polarised vasculature, which develops prior to SC migration (Cattin et al., 2015; Cattin and Lloyd, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SCs cultured alone exhibit contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL).
source: However, the collective migration of SCs as cords is an adaptive process, as SCs cultured alone exhibit contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL) (Parrinello et al., 2010), a process in which two cells repulse each other upon contact, resulting in the separation of cells (Abercrombie and Heaysman, 1953; Abercrombie and Heaysman, 1954; Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2008; Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work including the authors' own work.

claim: SC collective migration is triggered following interactions with fibroblasts that come into contact with SCs as they enter the wound site.
source: Following an injury, however, SC collective migration is triggered following interactions with fibroblasts that come into contact with SCs as they enter the wound site (Parrinello et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Heterotypic interaction with fibroblasts transforms SC behaviour from repulsive to attractive through ephrinB/EphB2 signalling inducing a Sox2-mediated re-localisation of N-cadherin to cell–cell junctions.
source: This heterotypic interaction with fibroblasts transforms SC behaviour from repulsive to attractive, a process mediated by ephrinB/EphB2 signalling inducing a Sox2-mediated re-localisation of N-cadherin to the site of cell–cell junctions, which results in SCs migrating as cellular cords (Parrinello et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: N-cadherin knockdown cells closed the gap more slowly in scratch assays and migrated in multiple directions over each other with a lack of persistent migration towards the gap.
source: Time-lapse microscopy showed that while scrambled control siRNA-treated cells migrated in a directional manner to efficiently close the gap, N-cadherin-knockdown cells closed the gap more slowly as they migrated in multiple directions over each other and with a lack of persistent migration towards the gap (Figure 1a–d).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1a-d.

claim: Individual N-cadherin-knockdown cells migrated more rapidly than control cells.
source: This difference was not due to a defect in migration speed as individual N-cadherin-knockdown cells migrated more rapidly (Figure 1e), suggesting that N-cadherin was required for the cell-contact-dependent process driving outward migration.
evidence: This is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Confluent control SCs form a monolayer and stable junctions, whereas N-cadherin knockdown cells were unable to form junctions and grew on top of each other.
source: Consistent with this, confluent control SCs form a monolayer and stable junctions, whereas N-cadherin knockdown cells were unable to form junctions and grew on top of each other (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: N-cadherin knockdown cells lost the ability to recognize each other.
source: This indicated N-cadherin knockdown cells had lost the ability to recognise each other, and that the loss of contact-dependent outward migration observed in the collective migration assay may be due to loss of CIL.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that N-cadherin knockdown cells grow on top of each other and lack directional migration.

claim: Control SCs retract their protrusions and change direction of migration upon contact with another SC.
source: Live imaging of siRNA scrambled control SCs showed that SCs migrate in multiple directions, making frequent, seemingly random, protrusions and retractions in multiple directions. However, upon contact with another SC, the SC nearly always retracts the contacting protrusion, appears repulsed, and changes its direction of migration (Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1f, quantified in Figure 1g), behaviours that are features of CIL (Abercrombie and Heaysman, 1953; Abercrombie and Heaysman, 1954) and is consistent with what we observed previously (Parrinello et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1f, g and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: N-cadherin knockdown cells continued to move forward upon contact and migrated on top of each other.
source: In contrast, while free-moving N-cadherin knockdown cells continued to make random protrusions and frequently changed direction, upon contact they behaved very differently to control cells, in that they continued to move forward upon contact and migrated on top of each other, a behaviour we termed overlapping.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1f, g.

claim: N-cadherin is required for CIL between collectively migrating SCs.
source: These results show that in addition to mediating adhesion between SCs, N-cadherin is also required for CIL between collectively migrating SCs.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including knockdown experiments and quantification of cell behavior shown in Figure 1.

claim: N-cadherin is required to present a repulsion signal and induce repulsion but is not required for a cell to be repulsed.
source: This suggested that N-cadherin is required to present a repulsion signal and induce repulsion but is not required for a cell to be repulsed.
evidence: This is supported by mixing experiments shown in Figure 2a, b where N-cadherin knockdown cells are repulsed by control cells.

claim: N-cadherin is only required to present a repulsion signal, but not to be repulsed.
source: This shows that N-cadherin is required to present a repulsion signal and induce repulsion, but not to be repulsed (Figure 2—video 1, Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by mixing experiments and dual-chamber assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: N-cadherin mediates CIL independent of trans-homodimerisation.
source: Moreover, it suggests that N-cadherin mediates CIL independent of trans-homodimerisation, implying a distinct mechanism mediates CIL.
evidence: This is inferred from the mixing experiments showing that N-cadherin is only required on one cell to mediate repulsion.

claim: α-catenin knockdown in SCs had no effect on CIL.
source: Time-lapse microscopy showed that efficient knockdown of α-catenin in SCs had no effect on CIL as the cells still repulsed each other despite an increase in cell velocity (Figure 2e and f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by CIL assays and velocity measurements shown in Figure 2e, f.

claim: SCs depleted of p120 catenin still repulsed each other upon contact.
source: Similarly, SCs depleted of p120 catenin still repulsed each other upon contact, although there was a slight but significant decrease in repulsive events in cells treated with siRNA2 (Figure 2g and h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is supported by CIL assays shown in Figure 2g, h.

claim: N-cadherin-mediated CIL is both independent of trans-homodimerisation and acts independently of the adherens junction complex.
source: Together these results indicated that N-cadherin-mediated CIL is both independent of trans-homodimerisation and acts independently of the adherens junction complex.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including mixing experiments and knockdown of adherens junction components shown in Figure 2.

claim: The extracellular domain of N-cadherin is sufficient to rescue CIL in N-cadherin knocked-down cells.
source: Strikingly, CIL was fully rescued by SCs expressing the extracellular domain of N-cadherin showing that intracellular signalling by N-cadherin is not required to mediate CIL (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3c, d.

claim: Glypican-4 knockdown cells did not repulse upon contact, nor did they invade; instead, they adhered to each other and formed clusters.
source: Intriguingly, Glypican-4 knockdown cells did not repulse upon contact, nor did they invade (Figure 4a). Instead, upon contact it appeared that the cells adhered to each other and formed clusters (Figure 4b and c, Figure 4—video 1), with cell velocity prior to cluster formation unaffected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by CIL assays and cluster formation assays shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: N-cadherin was still present at the membrane in Glypican-4 knockdown cells and accumulated at cell–cell contacts, forming more pronounced junctions compared to the control.
source: Consistent with this finding, N-cadherin was still present at the membrane in Glypican-4 knockdown cells with confocal images showing that N-cadherin accumulated at the cell–cell contacts, forming more pronounced junctions compared to the control (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Double knockdown of both Glypican-4 and N-cadherin resulted in cells that grew on top of each other, mimicking the N-cadherin knockdown phenotype.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, double knockdown of both Glypican-4 and N-cadherin resulted in cells that grew on top of each other, mimicking the N-cadherin knockdown phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e), highlighting the role for N-cadherin in presenting the repulsive signal, that is independent of its role at cell:cell junctions.
evidence: This is supported by double knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: Slit2 and Slit3 are predominately expressed by SCs.
source: Previous studies have shown that of the three Slit genes, Slit2 and Slit3 are predominately expressed by SCs (Carr et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2013). We first confirmed this finding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f and citations to previous literature.

claim: Slit2/Slit3 knockdown cells no longer repulsed upon contact and showed increased levels of adhesion.
source: We therefore performed a double knockdown of Slit2 and Slit3 and found that Slit2/Slit3 knockdown cells behaved similarly to Glypican-4 cells in that they no longer repulsed upon contact, showing instead, increased levels of adhesion (Figure 4d, Figure 4—video 2), resulting in the formation of cell clusters with increased N-cadherin-mediated junctions compared to the control (Figure 4e and f).
evidence: This is supported by CIL assays and cluster formation assays shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: Loss of either the Robo1 or Robo2 receptor in SCs resulted in a strong increase in cluster formation.
source: Similarly, to the Slit2/Slit3 KDs, loss of either the Robo1 or Robo2 receptor in SCs resulted in a strong increase in cluster formation (Figure 4g and h), which resembled the quieter, round clusters observed with Slit2/Slit3 and Glypican-4 KDs.
evidence: This is supported by cluster formation assays shown in Figure 4g, h.

claim: Slit2/Slit3 mediates the CIL signal through interactions with Robo1/2 and Glypican-4.
source: Together these results indicate that Slit2/Slit3 mediates the CIL signal through interactions with Robo1/2 and Glypican-4.
evidence: This is supported by knockdown experiments of Slit2/3, Robo1/2, and Glypican-4 shown in Figure 4.

claim: Overexpression of Sox2 resulted in polarised clusters of SCs with increased N-cadherin at the cell–cell contacts.
source: Overexpression of Sox2 resulted in polarised clusters of SCs with increased N-cadherin at the cell–cell contacts (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Clusters associated with Slit2/Slit3 knockdown consisted of more 'rounded' SCs, which lacked polarity.
source: In contrast, the clusters associated with Slit2/Slit3 knockdown had a very different morphology, consisting of more 'rounded' SCs, which lacked polarity, suggesting that the absence of Slit2/Slit3 signals between the cells results in cell clusters that lack an outward force to drive collective migration (Figure 4i, quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1i, and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification shown in Figure 4i and Figure 4—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Total Slit2 and Slit3 protein levels showed little change following N-cadherin knockdown.
source: However, following N-cadherin knockdown, little change was detected in total Slit2 and Slit3 protein levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) and mRNA levels of Slit2/3 and Glypican-4 were also not affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), indicating a post-translational mechanism was involved.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: Slit2 could be pulled down by N-cadherin in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments showed that Slit2 could be pulled down by N-cadherin (Figure 5c)
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In N-cadherin knockdown cells, Slit2 and Slit3 were no longer observable at the cell surface but rather were sequestered in the perinuclear region.
source: In contrast, in N-cadherin knockdown cells, Slit2 and Slit3 were no longer observable at the cell surface but rather were sequestered in the perinuclear region (Figure 5a and c and quantified in Figure 5b and d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification shown in Figure 5a-d.

claim: Slit2 and Slit3 localisation could be restored by expression of the extracellular domain of N-cadherin.
source: Importantly, Slit2 and Slit3 localisation could be restored by expression of the extracellular domain of N-cadherin (Figure 5e and g and quantified in Figure 5f and h).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5e-h.

claim: Slit2 and Slit3 were still observed at the cell surface in Glypican-4 knockdown cells.
source: In contrast, Slit2 and Slit3 were still observed at the cell surface in Glypican-4 knockdown cells, suggesting that Glypican-4 does not appear to be involved in trafficking Slit2/Slit3 to the cell surface but more likely has a role in stabilising the cell surface presentation, as indicated by previous studies (Ronca et al., 2001; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous literature.

claim: A pool of N-cadherin, via its extracellular domain, is required to facilitate Slit2 and Slit3 localisation at the cell surface.
source: Together these results show that a pool of N-cadherin, via its extracellular domain, is required to facilitate Slit2 and Slit3 localisation at the cell surface, where, together with Glypican-4, they mediate CIL.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including knockdown, rescue, and localization studies shown in Figure 5.

claim: Slit2/Slit3 knockdown decreased the collective migration of SCs.
source: To test if the Slit CIL signal is important for the collective migration of SCs, we performed a collective migration assay with Slit2/Slit3 KD SCs and found this was sufficient to decrease the collective migration of these cells (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a, and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by collective migration assays shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Recombinant Slit2 (rSlit2) inhibited Slit-mediated repulsion signalling, as rSlit2-treated SCs no longer repulsed each other and instead formed clusters.
source: To test this, we initially analysed the effect of rSlit2 on CIL in low-density cultures and found that rSlit2 inhibited Slit-mediated repulsion signalling, as rSlit2-treated SCs no longer repulsed each other and instead formed clusters (Figure 6b, quantified in Figure 6c, and Figure 6—video 2), similar to that observed when Slit signalling was inhibited using siRNA (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by CIL assays and cluster formation assays shown in Figure 6b, c.

claim: Cells treated with rSlit2 migrated less efficiently than controls in collective migration assays, with a slower closure of the gap.
source: Next, we performed a collective migration chamber assay in cells treated with rSlit2 and found that similar to the Slit2/Slit3 knockdowns, cells treated with rSlit2 migrated less efficiently than controls, with a slower closure of the gap (Figure 6d, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, and Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: This is supported by collective migration assays shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Addition of rSlit2 to Sox2-induced SC clusters resulted in clusters with a distinct morphology that were rounder and lacked polarisation.
source: Consistent with this, we found that the addition of rSlit2 to Sox2-induced SC clusters resulted in clusters with a distinct morphology (Figure 6g), in that the clusters were rounder (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d and e), and that the cells within the cluster lacked polarisation away from the cluster, as measured by both cell roundness (Figure 6h) and nuclear alignment (Figure 6i, Figure 6—figure supplement 1d), suggesting a lack of repulsion between the cells (Astin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification shown in Figure 6g-i.

claim: Loss of Slit2/Slit3 in Sox2-induced SC clusters resulted in the formation of large, round, clusters that lacked polarity.
source: Moreover, loss of Slit2/Slit3 in Sox2-induced SC clusters resulted in a similarly profound change in cluster morphology with the formation of large, round, clusters that lacked polarity in contrast to the polarised clusters of cells that form in response to Sox2 (Figure 6j, quantified in Figure 6k and Figure 6—figure supplement 1f and g).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification shown in Figure 6j, k.

claim: The outward force provided by Slit/Robo signalling is required for SC collective migration.
source: Together these findings indicate that the outward force provided by Slit/Robo signalling is required for SC collective migration and that inhibiting this signal results in the formation of non-polarised clusters of cells with limited migratory ability (Figure 6l).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches shown in Figure 6.

claim: At day 5 post-injury, SC cords are migrating into the newly formed nerve bridge.
source: Nerves were removed at day 5 following a transection injury, at which point SC cords are migrating into the new tissue formed at the injury site (the nerve bridge).
evidence: This is based on previous knowledge of nerve regeneration timing.

claim: The structure of the injured nerve was maintained ex vivo, with the bridge comprising of densely packed nuclei, with regrowing axons migrating with SC cords along the newly formed vasculature.
source: We observed that the structure of the injured nerve was maintained ex vivo, with the bridge comprising of densely packed nuclei, with regrowing axons migrating with SC cords along the newly formed vasculature (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and b), indicating that this is a powerful model in which we can visualise nerve regeneration ex vivo (Cattin et al., 2015; Parrinello et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo imaging data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: Treatment with rSlit2 resulted in an impairment of the collective migration of SCs in ex vivo explants, as evidenced by a decrease in the area of SC migration at 24 hr.
source: In contrast, treatment with rSlit2 resulted in an impairment of the collective migration of SCs, as evidenced by a decrease in the area of SC migration at 24 hr (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7c, d.

claim: Within rSlit2-treated nerves, there were significantly fewer SCs in polarised cords with the SCs instead found in clusters.
source: Moreover, within rSlit2-treated nerves, the SCs exhibited a distinct morphology in that there were significantly fewer SCs in polarised cords (Figure 7f) with the SCs instead, found in clusters, comparable in phenotype to those seen in vitro (Figure 7g).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7f, g.

claim: SCs treated with rSlit2 displayed a more rounded phenotype when compared to controls.
source: Further analysis of the SCs within the bridge, using Imaris to define the individual shape of the cells, showed that those treated with rSlit2 displayed a more rounded phenotype when compared to controls, consistent with the loss of CIL between the SCs, resulting in a loss of polarisation (Figure 7h and i).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction and quantification shown in Figure 7h, i.

claim: Control cords showed increased alignment of following cells to the leader cell, consistent with polarised collective migration.
source: As an additional measurement of persistence of directionality, we measured the alignment of the following cells to the leader cell and found increased alignment in the control cells, consistent with polarised collective migration (Figure 7j, Figure 7—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of nuclear alignment shown in Figure 7j.

claim: Control cords were more aligned as they migrated across the wound site, whereas the rSlit2-treated explants appeared to lose this directionality.
source: Moreover, we also found the control cords were more aligned as they migrated across the wound site, whereas the rSlit2-treated explants appeared to lose this directionality, resulting in SCs migrating in more random directions into the bridge (Figure 7k).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of SC persistence shown in Figure 7k.

claim: The Slit2-mediated CIL signal is essential for the effective migration of SC cords, which are essential for nerve regeneration.
source: Together, these findings confirm the importance of the Slit2-mediated CIL signal for the effective migration of SC cords, which are essential for nerve regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: N-cadherin acts at SC cell:cell junctions to mediate the formation of migratory SC cords, whilst acting as a mediator of the repulsive Slit/Robo CIL signal to provide the force required to drive the outward migration of the SC cords.
source: Moreover, these studies explain the apparently opposing dual roles for N-cadherin in the collective migration of SC during nerve regeneration, in that N-cadherin acts at SC cell:cell junctions to mediate the formation of migratory SC cords, whilst acting as a mediator of the repulsive Slit/Robo CIL signal to provide the force required to drive the outward migration of the SC cords that ensures successful nerve repair (Figure 7l).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: N-cadherin has previously been shown to mediate the repulsion signal important for the collective migration of neural crest cells.
source: N-cadherin has previously been shown to mediate the repulsion signal important for the collective migration of neural crest cells (Becker et al., 2013; Scarpa et al., 2015; Theveneau et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CIL between neural crest cells was reported to require the trans-homodimerisation of N-cadherin that acted to inhibit local protrusion formation at cell–cell contacts via the adherens complex.
source: However, despite neural crest cells and SCs belonging to the same lineage, we find that N-cadherin acts by a different mechanism to regulate CIL in SCs; CIL between neural crest cells was reported to require the trans-homodimerisation of N-cadherin that acted to inhibit local protrusion formation at cell–cell contacts via the adherens complex (Becker et al., 2013; Scarpa et al., 2015; Theveneau et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In SCs, while cell–cell adhesion is mediated by N-cadherin homodimers linked to the actin cytoskeleton via the adherens junction complex, N-cadherin mediates CIL by a distinct mechanism that does not require trans-homodimerisation, is independent of the adherens junction complex, and only requires the extracellular domain.
source: In contrast, in SCs, while cell–cell adhesion is mediated by N-cadherin homodimers linked to the actin cytoskeleton via the adherens junction complex, N-cadherin mediates CIL by a distinct mechanism. This does not require trans-homodimerisation, is independent of the adherens junction complex, and only requires the extracellular domain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Slits are secreted axonal guidance molecules that are crucial for the development of the brain.
source: Slits are secreted axonal guidance molecules that are crucial for the development of the brain (Blockus and Chédotal, 2014; Brose et al., 1999; Gonda et al., 2020; Jia et al., 2005; Kidd et al., 1999; Nguyen-Ba-Charvet et al., 2004; Ypsilanti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CIL between fibroblasts involves Slit2/Robo4 signalling.
source: However, while secreted, accumulating evidence suggests that the secreted forms can remain associated with the plasma membrane which would allow the local cell–cell signalling required for CIL (Blockus and Chedotal, 2016); indeed, it has been reported that CIL between fibroblasts involves Slit2/Robo4 signalling (Fritz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Slit2/Slit3 signalling is responsible for the homotypic CIL signal between SCs and this signal is required for the efficient directional collective SC migration that is required for nerve repair.
source: Here, we show that Slit2/Slit3 signalling is responsible for the homotypic CIL signal between SCs and that this signal is required for the efficient directional collective SC migration that is required for nerve repair.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figures 4, 6, and 7.

claim: Slit2, Slit3, and Robo1 are expressed by myelinating and non-myelinating SCs.
source: This is consistent with reports that Slit2, Slit3, and Robo1 are expressed by myelinating and non-myelinating SCs (Carr et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2013) and that a Slit2 signal can repulse a SC in culture (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Slit-dependent CIL between SCs requires both the extracellular domain of N-cadherin and Glypican-4.
source: Our work shows that Slit-dependent CIL between SCs requires both the extracellular domain of N-cadherin and Glypican-4, and it therefore appears likely that this complex is important for the localisation and retention of Slit2/Slit3 at the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Glypican and other heparan sulphate proteoglycans appear to be important for local Slit signalling.
source: This is consistent with previous reports in which Glypican and other heparan sulphate proteoglycans appear to be important for local Slit signalling (Liang et al., 1999; Piper et al., 2006; Ronca et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SCs show complex migratory behaviours influenced by the microenvironment; SCs alone exhibit CIL, which is a N-cadherin/Glypican4/Slit2/Slit3/Robo1/2-dependent process that repulse SCs from each other.
source: Further complexities of the role of CIL in cell behaviour are indicated by the distinct mechanisms used to regulate heterotypic and homotypic CIL and how these signals can change the migratory behaviour of cells. SCs show complex migratory behaviours influenced by the microenvironment; SCs alone exhibit CIL, which we now show is a N-cadherin/Glypican4/Slit2/Slit3/Robo1/2-dependent process that repulse SCs from each other, which is perhaps important for the distribution of SCs along axons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Following an injury, SCs come into contact with fibroblasts at the injury site and the fibroblasts repulse SCs by an ephrinB/EphB2–dependent signal.
source: Following an injury, however, SCs come into contact with fibroblasts at the injury site and the fibroblasts repulse SCs by an ephrinB/EphB2–dependent signal (Parrinello et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The ephrinB/EphB2 signal changes the behaviour of N-cadherin, resulting in the formation of more stable N-cadherin junctions via Sox2.
source: Importantly, this signal also changes the behaviour of N-cadherin, resulting in the formation of more stable N-cadherin junctions via Sox2.
evidence: This is based on previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Sox2-mediated stabilisation of N-cadherin at the cell–cell contacts acts dominantly over the CIL signal, resulting in the formation of cellular cords.
source: Critical to this interaction is the dual role of N-cadherin in SC migration, with Sox2-mediated stabilisation of N-cadherin at the cell–cell contacts found to act dominantly over the CIL signal, resulting in the formation of cellular cords.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous work.

claim: Within the cords, the Slit2/Slit3-dependent repulsion signal remains active, providing an outward force to drive the collective migration of these cells.
source: However, within the cords, the Slit2/Slit3-dependent repulsion signal remains active, providing an outward force to drive the collective migration of these cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Loss of N-cadherin results in the production of overlapping, highly migratory cells that lack collective behaviour.
source: So, whereas loss of N-cadherin results in the production of overlapping, highly migratory cells that lack collective behaviour, inhibition of Slit2/Slit3 results in the formation of tighter clusters of cells associated with enhanced N-cadherin junctions in which migration is inhibited (Figure 6k).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figures 1 and 6.

claim: Inhibition of Slit2/Slit3 results in the formation of tighter clusters of cells associated with enhanced N-cadherin junctions in which migration is inhibited.
source: So, whereas loss of N-cadherin results in the production of overlapping, highly migratory cells that lack collective behaviour, inhibition of Slit2/Slit3 results in the formation of tighter clusters of cells associated with enhanced N-cadherin junctions in which migration is inhibited (Figure 6k).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Targeting of CIL signals would be a promising approach for inhibiting unwanted collective migration.
source: This might suggest targeting of CIL signals would be a promising approach for inhibiting unwanted collective migration.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Exogenous recombinant Slit2 (rSlit2) acts to inhibit SC CIL and inhibits the collective migration of these cells.
source: Consistent with this, we showed that exogenous recombinant Slit2 (rSlit2) acts to inhibit SC CIL and inhibits the collective migration of these cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figure 6.
